title.rendered: Penang Bridge ruling shows why the first days on site matter most

content.rendered:
In February 2021, fire damaged the Penang Bridge, one of Malaysia’s most important pieces of public infrastructure. More than five years later, the High Court of Malaya has ruled on its cause, ordering Tenaga Nasional to pay RM10.5 million (US$2.6 million) to Projek Lebuhraya Usahasama.

The court heard two explanations. One was that an external rubbish fire, started by a discarded cigarette, was to blame. The other was that electrical arcing, associated with existing mechanical damage to high-voltage cables, caused the fire. The court rejected the first and accepted the second.

Having given evidence that played a key role in the court’s assessment, I believe the court’s reasoning holds a clear lesson for insurers and claims professionals across the region: early evidence capture is critical in complex fire losses.

The scene is the evidence

The court placed significant weight on evidence gathered during the immediate site investigation. I attended the scene with an electrical engineer, and we examined and documented the physical evidence before site conditions changed. That evidence matched automated fault records and was supported by damage observed on surviving cable sheaths.

That combination matters. A theory can seem persuasive on paper long after an event, but a conclusion based on direct physical examination and tested against independent data carries weight.

Moreover, investigation scenes are often quickly altered post-event: debris is cleared, structures are made safe, repairs start, and weather takes over. Once this occurs, critical questions in disputes often can’t be answered.

Early attendance should be standard practice

Sometimes, forensic attendance on complex losses is treated as a discretionary cost, commissioned only once a dispute looks likely. By then, it can be too late. International forensic standards recognise that the treatment of an incident scene predetermines the quality and quantity of information later available as evidence in court.

The scene should therefore be recorded before anything changes. That means agreeing with the parties that clearance and repairs wait until it has been documented and relevant items retained, with a clear chain of custody.

Fault records, maintenance logs and system data can corroborate physical findings, so they should be requested early in proceedings.

Above all, the investigation must stay evidence-led, capturing everything, including what does not fit the expected explanation. Any gaps are exactly what another expert will find.

This doesn’t just apply to cases that end up in court. Most disputes settle, and parties negotiating from well-documented evidence are in a stronger position to reach a fair outcome.

A high bar for infrastructure operators

The decision also reinforces the high standard of care associated with managing high-voltage electrical infrastructure. Where those systems sit alongside public assets such as a major bridge, the consequences of failure extend well beyond the operator.

For insurers on both sides of such risks, the condition and maintenance of electrical systems will be central to any causation dispute. That evidence, too, is best captured early.

Getting it right at the start

This matter demonstrates why early attendance can be critical in complex fire investigations. Examining and documenting physical evidence at the scene provides a stronger foundation for understanding what occurred and for assisting the court.

Desktop analysis and expert debate have their place. But they are only as good as the evidence underneath them, and that evidence is at its most complete in the first days after a loss.

Anand Ghnavello is director of forensic services for Asia at Halliwell and is a certified fire and explosion investigator.

title.rendered: Zurich, Allianz JD, Howden, McLarens: 8 APAC insurance people moves of the week

content.rendered:
InsuranceAsia News wraps up the people moves from the insurance industry in Asia this week.

1. Zurich names China unit CEO, greater China CFO

Zurich Insurance has named Scott Yin as CEO of its China unit.

Yin will take charge of the growth of Zurich’s commercial insurance business and the ongoing expansion of its retail business, including Zurich Cover-More, its Travel Guard offering in the Chinese Market.

Zurich Insurance has handed Hong Kong CFO Martin Noble an additional role as chief financial officer for greater China.

In the expanded role, Noble will be responsible for strengthening collaboration between Zurich’s  Hong Kong and China finance teams, enhancing coordination in financial management, accounting and treasury activities.

Read the full story here and here.

2. Allianz Jingdong appoints new CEO

John Chen has replaced William Liang as chief executive officer for Allianz Jingdong General Insurance (Allianz JD), the German insurer’s joint venture in China with Chinese e-commerce firm JD.com.

Liang left Allianz JD on Thursday to pursue new opportunities, while Chen’s appointment is effective from Friday.

Read the full story here.

3. Howden Australia builds out sport, entertainment practice, appoints Pacific head of technical, claims

Howden Australia has added five senior ex-Marsh brokers to grow its sport and entertainment practice, which it called “a significant investment in the sector.”

Simon Calabrese has been appointed as head of leisure and entertainment, while Lauren Coburn, Sarah Collin, Melissa Fitzsimmons and James Schubach have been tapped as senior associates for the division.

Gold Coast-based Calabrese brings over two decades of experience in the business line, including eight years at Marsh and JLT and 16 years at Aon.

Catherine Osbourne has been named as the firm’s new head of technical and claims in the Pacific.

Sydney-based Osbourne has joined Howden from Marsh, where she was chief claims officer for the Pacific region from January 2022 until April.

Read the full story here and here.

4. McLarens’ adjuster swaps Sydney for Singapore, handed regional role

McLarens has appointed Nathan Baran as regional loss adjuster, based in Singapore.

Baran has relocated from Sydney, where he was most recently an executive liability loss adjuster since April 2025.

Read the full story here.

5. BMS Group taps executive broker in New Zealand

Global broker BMS Group has appointed Grant Robertson as an executive broker within its New Zealand business.

Robertson joins from Donaldson Brown in Auckland, where he spent over eight years in roles including head of financial lines and international placements and head of complex risks.

Read the full story here.

6. Parametric specialist IBISA appoints India CEO

Luxembourg-headquartered parametric insurtech IBISA has appointed Samdarshi Vikram Singh as CEO for India to drive its next growth phase.

Singh joins from Generali Central, where he has worked for nearly a decade, most recently as the head of government business and reinsurance.

Read the full story here.

7. Allianz Australia hires senior liability underwriter

Stephanie Roth has rejoined Allianz Australia as a senior liability underwriter.

Perth-based Roth joins from Liberty Specialty Markets, where she spent over five years, most recently as a senior casualty underwriter since October 2024.

Read the full story here.

8. Generali Central Insurance appoints CFO

Generali Central Insurance has appointed Chandraprakash Jain as chief financial officer (designate). 

Mumbai-based Jain has over two decades of experience across finance, insurance, accounting, strategic planning, mergers and acquisitions, and business operations.

Read the full story here.
